opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. It's funny, because quadratic reciprocity is something a lot of mathematicians remember as their first real love, and I think there's a reason for that.

At Ross, they don't just hand you the theorem. You spend weeks working through problem sets on number theory from scratch: modular arithmetic, primes, what it means for a number to be a square mod p. You're grinding through examples by hand, filling notebooks with tables of residues. And you start noticing patterns you can't explain. Whether 3 is a square mod 7 seems to be related, in a strange way, to whether 7 is a square mod 3. You think: why on earth would these two questions talk to each other? They live in completely different worlds.

Then you get to quadratic reciprocity, and it says yes, there is a precise, beautiful law connecting them, with just a little sign twist depending on whether the primes are 1 or 3 mod 4. For me that was the moment. It wasn't that the statement was complicated. It was that it was so simple, and so unexpected. It felt like discovering that two strangers on opposite sides of the world had been secretly writing to each other the whole time.

And the proofs! Gauss found many proofs, and there's this sense that the truth is so robust you can approach it from many directions: counting lattice points, Gauss's lemma, Gauss sums. Each one shows you a different face of the same thing. As a teenager, that gave me the feeling that mathematics isn't a collection of tricks. There's a hidden structure, and proof is how you get to touch it.

Ross's motto is "think deeply of simple things," and quadratic reciprocity is exactly that. You start with something as humble as squaring numbers and taking remainders, and if you stay with it long enough, it opens into something profound. I think a lot of what I've done since, including caring so much about proof and about what it means to really know something is true, traces back to that summer.

r001.rationale: She contrasts the theorem’s simple, unexpected statement with its many approaches to proof, saying this revealed hidden mathematical structure and gave her a sense of wonder.

fable-5.1.text:
I remember it really clearly. At Ross, you don't get told things. You sit with a problem set and you compute. So for weeks we were just playing with squares modulo primes, by hand, filling in these tables of which numbers are quadratic residues mod 3, mod 5, mod 7, mod 11, and so on. It felt like bookkeeping. I didn't think there was anything there.

And then at some point you line the tables up and you ask, when is p a square mod q, and when is q a square mod p, and you notice they almost always answer the same way. And the only time they don't is when both primes are 3 mod 4. That's the whole law. One sentence. But it connects two questions that have no business talking to each other. Whether 7 is a square mod 11 should be a fact about the world mod 11. Whether 11 is a square mod 7 should be a fact about the world mod 7. There's no shared structure you can see. And yet they know about each other.

That was the moment for me. It wasn't that the statement was hard, it was that the statement was true for no reason I could point to. Gauss called it the golden theorem and gave something like eight proofs, and I think that's because the proofs didn't really explain it either. Each one made it true but none of them made it obvious. Later I learned that the real explanation sits much higher up, in class field theory and in how primes split in extensions, and that quadratic reciprocity is sort of the shadow of that cast onto the integers.

So what struck me was this feeling that mathematics has hidden layers. The numbers you can touch are the surface, and there are things underneath that you can't see directly but that leave fingerprints on the surface. Before that I thought math was about being clever. After that I thought math was about discovering that something is already there, and that was a completely different kind of motivation. I think I've been chasing that feeling ever since.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the law’s one-sentence statement with Gauss’s many proofs, saying none made it obvious, and identifies that contrast as part of what struck Hong.

astra-6.text:
I think it was the surprise that a question so simple could have such a deep answer. You ask whether one prime is a square modulo another prime, and then you reverse the roles of the two primes. At first, those seem like separate questions. Quadratic reciprocity tells you they’re connected in this incredibly precise way.

And at Ross, you’re spending time working through examples and trying to understand why things are true. So the theorem becomes more than a beautiful statement—you start to see the structure behind it. That connection between something very concrete and something unexpectedly deep was what really struck me.

sol-6.1.text: I think it was the surprise that something so simple to state could have such a deep pattern behind it. You start with a very concrete question—when is one number a square modulo a prime?—and then quadratic reciprocity connects two of those questions in this unexpected, beautiful way. At Ross, spending time working toward a proof made that connection feel earned. It was a glimpse of how mathematics can take something that looks mysterious and make it feel inevitable.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a simple-to-state result with the deep pattern behind it and says working toward a proof at Ross made the connection feel earned, presenting that contrast as a source of wonder.
